verses.text: Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel, and said to them, “These are the words which Yahweh has commanded, that you should do them.
‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day there shall be a holy day for you, a Sabbath of solemn rest to Yahweh: whoever does any work in it shall be put to death.
You shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations on the Sabbath day.’”
Moses spoke to all the congregation of the children of Israel, saying, “This is the thing which Yahweh commanded, saying,
‘Take from among you an offering to Yahweh. Whoever is of a willing heart, let him bring it, Yahweh’s offering: gold, silver, brass,
blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair,
rams’ skins dyed red, sea cow hides, acacia wood,
oil for the light, spices for the anointing oil and for the sweet incense,
onyx stones, and stones to be set for the ephod and for the breastplate.
“‘Let every wise-hearted man among you come, and make all that Yahweh has commanded:
the tabernacle, its outer covering, its roof, its clasps, its boards, its bars, its pillars, and its sockets;
the ark, and its poles, the mercy seat, the veil of the screen;
the table with its poles and all its vessels, and the show bread;
the lamp stand also for the light, with its vessels, its lamps, and the oil for the light;
and the altar of incense with its poles, the anointing oil, the sweet incense, the screen for the door, at the door of the tabernacle;
the altar of burnt offering, with its grating of brass, it poles, and all its vessels, the basin and its base;
the hangings of the court, its pillars, their sockets, and the screen for the gate of the court;
the pins of the tabernacle, the pins of the court, and their cords;
the finely worked garments, for ministering in the holy place, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, to minister in the priest’s office.’”
All the congregation of the children of Israel departed from the presence of Moses.

They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought Yahweh’s offering, for the work of the Tent of Meeting, and for all of its service, and for the holy garments.

They came, both men and women, as many as were willing-hearted, and brought brooches, earrings, signet rings, and armlets, all jewels of gold; even every man who offered an offering of gold to Yahweh.
Everyone, with whom was found blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, and sea cow hides, brought them.
Everyone who offered an offering of silver and brass brought Yahweh’s offering; and everyone, with whom was found acacia wood for any work of the service, brought it.
All the women who were wise-hearted spun with their hands, and brought that which they had spun, the blue, the purple, the scarlet, and the fine linen.
All the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun the goats’ hair.
The rulers brought the onyx stones, and the stones to be set, for the ephod and for the breastplate;
and the spice, and the oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the sweet incense.
The children of Israel brought a freewill offering to Yahweh; every man and woman, whose heart made them willing to bring for all the work, which Yahweh had commanded to be made by Moses.
Moses said to the children of Israel, “Behold, Yahweh has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
He has filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship;
and to make skillful works, to work in gold, in silver, in brass,
in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of skillful workmanship.
He has put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.

He has filled them with wisdom of heart, to work all kinds of workmanship, of the engraver, of the skillful workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, even of those who do any workmanship, and of those who make skillful works.

footnotes.content: Moses gathered the whole people to speak plainly about what God had commanded. There's something moving about how he brings everyone together before asking for anything—no hierarchy, no secrets, just the leader making sure all of God's family hears the same truth. That's where real obedience begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six days of work, one day of rest—and the Sabbath is so holy that breaking it costs a life. This isn't bureaucracy; it's God's way of saying we are not machines, and time set apart belongs only to Him. Even in the midst of building His dwelling place, the rhythm of rest cannot be broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No fire, no work—not even the warmth of a hearth on the Sabbath. The Israelites worked with fire constantly in their crafts and cooking, so this prohibition hit home. God is teaching them that Sabbath means complete trust: I will care for you without your labor, without even the comfort of your own making.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses repeats the word of the Lord formally, making it clear that what follows comes from God Himself, not from Moses' own leadership preferences. That honesty—'this is what He said'—creates the trust that allows hearts to respond with genuine willingness rather than mere obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Whoever is of a willing heart." God doesn't demand; He invites the generous to step forward. Notice the gold and silver and precious metals—these are things people treasure and hold tight. The Lord is asking His redeemed people to offer what they love most, and He does it gently, appealing to the awakened heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blues, purples, scarlets, fine linen—the very colors that will make the tabernacle beautiful. But these dyes were expensive and prized, marks of wealth and taste. By asking for them, God is saying: I want your very best, the things you've carefully preserved. Your treasure becomes His sanctuary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sea cow hides and acacia wood—practical materials from the wilderness itself. The acacia was native to the Sinai, strong and reliable. God isn't asking for impossibilities; He asks for what His people already possess, transformed into something holy by their willing devotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oil for the lamp, spices for anointing—the fragrance and light of God's presence. Someone has to give up their oil, their precious perfumes. They don't just give things; they give what sustains their own homes and bodies, so that God's house might be fragrant and illumined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Onyx and precious stones for the ephod and breastplate—stones that will sit on the priest's heart as he ministers. Beauty and purpose woven together: the stones are not just decoration but speak of God's value placed on the work of intercession. People give their best gems so the priest's burden becomes His glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Every wise-hearted man." Wisdom here isn't mere intelligence but moral vision—the ability to see what God is doing and join in. The Lord calls for skillful hands guided by hearts awake to His purposes. Craft married to conviction: that's the master-builder God seeks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inventory tumbles out: boards and bars, the ark and mercy seat, the table and lamp stand, the altar and veil. Each item has a purpose in God's dwelling; nothing is ornament-only. The detailed listing shows that God cares about order, function, and the specific structure of worship. He hasn't left the design vague—He knows exactly what His house needs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses finishes speaking, and the people leave his presence. No haggling, no committee formed to discuss it. There's a quiet obedience here—they've heard the Lord's word through Moses and they go, ready to respond. The heart's willingness to do what God asks often requires no lengthy deliberation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Everyone whose heart stirred him up"—stirred by whom? By the Holy Spirit, awakening generosity in the redeemed. The spirit makes us willing; willing hearts move us to give. Notice that people bring of their own motion; no one is conscripted. God's best work flows from hearts He has already touched.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men and women both, bringing their personal jewelry—brooches, rings, earrings, the adornments that marked them as people of substance. Families pooled their wealth without reservation. It's a picture of complete covenant: every person, every resource, given to build the place where they will meet with God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whoever had these materials brought them. The phrase suggests a community-wide search: 'Do you have blue fabric? Scarlet? Sea cow hides?' Neighbors asked neighbors, families inventoried their stores. The project became everyone's work before a hammer was ever swung.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver, brass, acacia wood—the practical metals and materials, the wood that would form the structure. Not every offering is visibly beautiful, but every honest offering carries weight. The Lord accepts both the glitter of the gems and the solid bulk of timber needed to hold the walls upright.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wise-hearted women, hands working the spindle, producing threads in blue and purple and scarlet. Their skill and labor go into these colors that will make the tabernacle shine. Craftsmanship is prayer; every thread spun is an act of worship and devotion to the God they serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The women whose hearts were stirred spun goats' hair. Not glamorous work—coarse fiber, steady hands, no quick result. Yet this humble labor becomes part of the sacred structure. God notices both the rare jewel and the long hours at the spindle; both serve His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rulers brought the onyx stones. Leadership means bearing the heavier responsibility, giving the costlier gifts first. The rulers set the tone of generosity so that all Israel would follow. Authority without sacrifice has no credibility; their offering sanctioned the whole project.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Spice and oil for light and anointing—things that make a house feel like home, that mark a space as set apart and blessed. The rulers brought these precious things alongside the stones, showing that even those of standing understood: all of it matters, nothing given is less than holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man and woman, from the youngest to the eldest, every heart that was willing brought a freewill offering. This is the model of a people genuinely called and responding: not coercion, but conviction; not taxation, but love. The tabernacle rose on the wings of voluntary devotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bezalel—'in the shadow of God'—is called by name. God doesn't work with anonymous labor; He sees the gifted craftsman and speaks his name aloud before the assembly. To have the Lord publicly recognize your gift is to know that your skill is not accident but calling, and that He has chosen you for a specific, sacred purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Filled with the Spirit of God—in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and workmanship. Notice the order: Spirit first, then knowledge flows. Bezalel's skill isn't merely human talent; it's the Holy Spirit working through him, making his hands an instrument of divine wisdom. All true craft is prayer made visible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold, silver, brass, stone-cutting, wood-carving, all kinds of skillful work—Bezalel's hands can do what no single craft demands. He is not one-trick, but rounded in artistry, able to move between materials and techniques. The Spirit gives breadth; the person brings faithfulness to learn and master each new thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord has put in his heart that he may teach—not just to make, but to pass on the gift. Bezalel isn't a lone genius but a guide to other artisans. He and Oholiab will train hands and eyes throughout Israel. The greatest gift a craftsperson can receive is the burden and joy of teaching others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Filled with wisdom of heart—wisdom sits in the heart, not the head alone. Bezalel and Oholiab embody the full range of the craftsperson's art: engraver, embroiderer, weaver, those who design and those who execute. Wisdom of heart means each one sees their own work as part of the whole, their skill as a thread in God's larger tapestry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
